title: Qualify a digital PID realization on the positioning table
physicalPurpose: Execute the same continuous PID intent on a sampled controller without allowing discretization, held output, quantization, aliasing, or computation delay to invalidate the design.
principalTechnique: Forward Euler, backward Euler, and Tustin digital realization
objective: Calculate and execute forward-Euler, backward-Euler, and Tustin realizations at several controller intervals, then decide which cases remain credible from actual sampling, held torque, tracking, quantization, aliasing, precision, and computation-delay evidence.

simplifications: The simulator advances the rigid joint every 10 ms while the controller may update less frequently.
A deterministic 8 Hz sinusoid and 0.001 rad quantizer isolate sampling effects; they are not a full physical encoder spectrum.
Controller arithmetic uses LREAL; processor execution-time distribution and missed deadlines are deferred to production timing lessons.

baseline.limitation: The fastest Tustin run is not evidence that Euler alternatives, slower updates, quantized measurements, aliased interference, or delayed application remain acceptable.

change.decision: Accept only a method and interval whose actual update timing, held output, tracking, torque, finite-state, quantization, alias, and delay evidence satisfy the declared requirements.

acceptance.window: 100 ms controller samples from 5 to 20 s

safety.restorationMode: Disable control and command zero torque after supporting the payload
simulationOnlyRestrictions: Simulated timing and sinusoidal encoder interference do not qualify physical task jitter, processor load, drive latency, encoder spectrum, or machine stability.

video.viewerOutcome: Calculate and choose a digital controller method and interval while recognizing hold, quantization, aliasing, precision, and computation-delay effects.
requiredVisibleEvidence: independently estimated 2 Hz alias from 8 Hz interference

learning.context: The same positioning table runs on a 10 ms plant step while a lesson-specific digital PID updates every 10, 20, or 100 ms and holds torque between updates.
learning.reason: The preceding lessons exposed sampling, filtering, actuator, and transmission effects; continuous gains alone cannot specify which samples, coefficients, held values, or delays the computer executes.
theory: Controller sample interval dt is elapsed time in seconds between controller updates. Sampling frequency f_s is updates per second and equals one divided by dt. Nyquist frequency f_N is half the sampling frequency.

Zero-order hold retains the last calculated torque between controller updates. Quantization step q is the 0.001 rad spacing between encoder values. Computation delay T_delay is one complete controller update when enabled.

Forward Euler accumulates the previous error and advances the filtered derivative from its previous measurement-rate input. Backward Euler uses current error and current position change. Tustin averages previous and current error and applies the trapezoidal mapping to the filtered derivative.

Filtered derivative torque T_D is the damping contribution calculated from measurement-rate change through a 0.05 s dynamic filter. The proportional, integral, and derivative torque contributions use identical continuous gains in every candidate.

Alias frequency f_alias is the lower sampled frequency produced when interference exceeds Nyquist. At 100 ms, 8 Hz interference sampled at 10 Hz appears at 2 Hz. LREAL provides coefficient and state precision but does not restore information lost to sampling or sensor quantization.
learning.workedPrediction: For dt values 0.01, 0.02, and 0.10 s, calculate f_s as 100, 50, and 10 Hz, f_N as 50, 25, and 5 Hz, and 100, 50, and 10 samples per 1 s mechanical velocity time constant. Calculate integral weights 0.02, 0.04, and 0.20; forward derivative coefficients 0.2, 0.4, and 2.0; backward denominators 1.2, 1.4, and 3.0; and Tustin retained-state coefficients 0.818, 0.667, and 0. At dt 0.10 s, the 8 Hz encoder component aliases to 2 Hz and one-update delay is 0.10 s.
practicalPreparation: Bind update pulse, setpoint, measured and ideal position, motor velocity, held requested and applied torque, method, interval, quantization step, interference frequency, and delay state.
Freeze gains, filter time constant, plant, initial state, noise phase, duration, limits, and seed before comparing methods or intervals.
learning.baseline: Run Tustin at 10 ms with no added computation delay; retain every base scan and actual controller update timestamp.
learning.change: At 20 ms compare forward Euler, backward Euler, and Tustin. Then hold Tustin and continuous parameters fixed while testing 10, 20, and 100 ms, followed by the one-update delay case.
learning.comparison: Compare position error, overshoot, settling status, torque total variation, update interval and jitter, held-output duration, quantization, sampled interference spectrum, and finite/bounded state on equal axes.
learning.validation: Require torque to change only on update pulses, selected intervals to match actual timestamps, measured position to remain on the 0.001 rad grid, and the retained 100 ms samples to independently estimate the dominant alias between 1.9 and 2.1 Hz. A settled case must permanently remain within the PV band and satisfy the final-window PV and torque spans. Require all states and torque to remain finite and bounded; label any unstable or nonsettling response honestly.
learning.explanation: The methods approximate the same continuous dynamics with different sample choices. Slower updates lengthen the hold and delay, alter coefficients, reduce the observable frequency range, and can make high-frequency content appear falsely slow.
learning.transfer: Select method and interval from plant bandwidth, noise, required phase margin, timing evidence, and numerical range. Lesson 26 uses this digital foundation to compare positional, incremental, and combined production PID forms.
